title: Learning How to Learn
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Ask a group of students how they revise and most will give the same answer: they read their notes again, and they highlight the important parts. These habits feel productive, and they are popular because they are easy. Yet psychologists who have compared study methods for decades rank rereading and highlighting among the least effective ways to learn. The methods that work best tend to be less comfortable, and for that reason fewer students choose them.

The first of these is retrieval practice, which simply means testing yourself on material instead of looking at it again. In a well-known experiment, Dr Katherine Doyle asked two groups of students to study a short science text. One group read it four times. The other read it once and then wrote down everything they could remember. A week later, the second group recalled about half as much again as the first, even though they had spent less time with the text. Strangely, the students who had reread the text felt more confident that they knew it.

The second method is spacing, which means spreading study over several days instead of cramming it into one long session. Memory fades quickly at first and then more slowly, and each time a person recalls something just as it starts to slip away, the memory becomes stronger and lasts longer. Three study sessions of an hour, on different days, will produce better results than a single three-hour session the night before a test, although the cramming student may feel well prepared at the time.

The third method is called interleaving. Most textbooks present one type of problem at a time, so that students practise a skill twenty times in a row before moving on. Professor Marcus Webb compared this with a mixed approach, in which different kinds of mathematics problem were shuffled together. During the practice sessions, the students who practised one type at a time made fewer mistakes. A week later, however, in a test, the students who had practised a mixture solved roughly twice as many problems correctly. Webb explains that mixing forces the learner to decide which method a problem needs, and that deciding is exactly what an examination demands.

Why do students avoid techniques that work? Psychologists point to what they call the illusion of fluency. When material is familiar, because we have just read it or because we have just practised the same skill, it feels easy, and we mistake that feeling for learning. Effortful methods are slower and produce more errors, and so they feel like failures. Researchers describe the extra effort as a 'desirable difficulty': a challenge that makes learning harder in the short term but better in the long term.

Teachers can help by building these methods into lessons. Short, frequent quizzes, which count for little or nothing towards a final grade, give students regular practice at retrieval. Homework that returns to topics from earlier in the term supplies spacing, and a worksheet that mixes several kinds of question supplies interleaving. Some teachers worry that frequent testing will make their students anxious, but studies suggest that low-stakes quizzes actually reduce anxiety, because students become used to being tested.

For students working alone, the advice is simple. Close the book and write down what you remember before you check your notes. Make flashcards, and go through them again after a day, a few days and a week. Return to old topics instead of leaving them behind, and mix different kinds of exercise in a single session. None of this will feel as pleasant as reading a neat page of highlighted notes, but, as the research shows, it is the discomfort that does the work.
